paper_title: Playing to Par: Reinforcement Learning for Provably Optimal Quadrilateral Block Decompositions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A quadrilateral block decomposition of a planar domain is judged by whether it is complete, whether its elements are well shaped, and how many of its vertices are irregular. The last has a provable floor: the discrete Gauss-Bonnet identity enforces a lower bound on the total vertex irregularity of any all-quadrilateral mesh of a given domain purely based on its topology and corner angles. We train a reinforcement learning agent to build decompositions that reach this bound, which we call par. It acts directly on the mesh's half-edge data structure through local edits, with a policy network whose convolutions follow the mesh's own connectivity, so it applies unchanged to domains larger than any seen in training. The reward targets the floor directly, and it is sparse: random play reaches it on no domain with more than eight sides. We overcome this exploration barrier via behaviour cloning on optimal meshes that are trivial to construct, walked backward into demonstrations, before training it with PPO. On 96 held-out domains the agent produces an all-quadrilateral mesh on every one, a usable one on 95.7 on average, and a provably optimal one on 90; Gmsh's strongest configuration at the same element count completes 51, is usable on 38 and optimal on none, and even at three to fourteen times the elements never produces a more regular mesh. On 64 domains twice the training size the agent completes all, is usable on 62, and keeps a median excess over par below one against Gmsh's 39 at the same element count.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: A quadrilateral block decomposition of planar domain is judged by whether it is complete, whether its elements are well shaped, and how many of its vertices are irregular. The last has provable floor: the discrete GaussBonnet identity enforces lower bound on the total vertex irregularity of any all-quadrilateral mesh of given domain purely based on its topology and corner angles. We train reinforcement learning agent to build decompositions that reach this bound, which we call par. It acts directly on the meshs half-edge data structure through local edits, with policy network whose convolutions follow the meshs own connectivity, so it applies unchanged to domains larger than any seen in training. The reward targets the floor directly, and it is sparse: random play reaches it on no domain with more than eight sides. We overcome this exploration barrier via behaviour cloning on optimal meshes that are trivial to construct, walked backward into demonstrations, before training it with PPO. On 96 held-out domains the agent produces an all-quadrilateral mesh on every one, usable one on 95.7 on average, and provably optimal one on 90; Gmshs strongest configuration at the same element count completes 51, is usable on 38 and optimal on none, and even at three to fourteen times the elements never produces more regular mesh. On 64 domains twice the training size the agent completes all, is usable on 62, and keeps median excess over par below one against Gmshs 39 at the same element count.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A block decomposition is coarse all-quadrilateral partition of domain with as regular vertex connectivity as the domain allows. Connectivity is crucial: thin element can be smoothed or split, but vertex of the wrong valence is singularity that survives every refinement. Structured and multi-block discretisations, tensor-product bases and subdivision all rely on regular connectivity (Bommes et al., 2013; Armstrong et al., 2015); production meshers clean up valence after the fact (Kinney, 1997), and advancing fronts introduce more singularities than domain needs, though topology makes some unavoidable (Armstrong et al., 2015; Fogg et al., 2018). Block decompositions are still built largely by hand or by heuristics, and often do not target optimality. That optimality criterion exists. The discrete GaussBonnet identity gives every domain lower bound on the irregularity of any all-quadrilateral mesh of it, computed from the domains corner angles and topology alone (Section 2). We call it par. It is computed once per domain before any mesh exists, and decomposition that reaches it is provably optimal in its connectivity. That makes block decomposition an unusual reinforcement learning (RL) problem: the reward is sparse, but success carries certificate. The sparsity is severe. We pose the problem as an MDP whose state is half-edge mesh and whose actions are four local operations (Section 3); uniform random play reaches par on about three percent of fiveand six-sided polygons and on none with more than eight sides, and policy trained from scratch rarely leaves that regime. We overcome this exploration barrier by behaviour cloning on known optimal trajectories, and continuing with reinforcement learning. The policy is convolution on the half-edge structure (Section 4): each half-edge receives messages from its next, 1 Figure 1: Our agent and Gmsh on the same three domains. Top: an in-distribution domain (chamfered, with hole, 18 corners). Middle: larger-boundary domain (38 corners), beyond any seen in training. Bottom: curved domain with holes (33 corners); the agent was never trained on curved boundary, and quality is given against the arc tangents and on chords (Section 6.4). Gmsh BLOSSOM is asked for our element count and returns the closest it can reach; QUASI-STRUCTURED runs at its natural size. Every irregular vertex is marked. Our top mesh has none, which the GaussBonnet bound (Section 2) certifies as optimal; the middle one has one, against 32 and 16 for Gmsh, and the curved one 15, against 64 and 35. Domains are chosen by the rule of Appendix M, which shows one per family. previous and twin, the pointers that define local topological connectivity. The input features and state representation are designed to allow the agent to scale to larger meshes than seen during training. Unlike prior reinforcement learning for block decomposition (Narayanan et al., 2024), whose half-edge framework we build on and which edits an existing all-quadrilateral mesh toward ideal vertex degrees, our agent starts from the bare boundary, targets bound computed from the domain, includes element quality in its reward, and overcomes the sparse reward by cloning. We also evaluate more comprehensively: on domains with holes, on domains twice the training size and on curved boundaries, against the production mesher Gmsh. Contributions. (i) An action space and policy network that operate directly on the half-edge data structure of any unstructured polygonal tiling. (ii) GEO2D, seeded generator and scoring protocol of mechanical-part outlines with chamfers, fillets, and holes, released as benchmark suite. (iii) training recipe for the sparse reward: shaped reward that targets par directly and is normalised so that returns share one scale across domain sizes; and optimal meshes that are trivial to construct, such as polyominoes, walked backward into verified demonstrations in the agents action space. Cloning on them overcomes the exploration barrier that otherwise blocks PPO.

sections.title: 3.1 STATES AND OBSERVATIONS
sections.content: We represent mesh by doubly connected edge list (DCEL): every edge carries two oppositely oriented half-edges, and all connectivity is expressed through three pointers per half-edge next and previous, which walk face loop counter-clockwise, and twin, which crosses to the adjoining face (Figure 2a). Holes enter through slit joining each hole boundary to the outer one, so multiply connected domain is still single face loop. state of the MDP is the current mesh together with the half-edge on which the observation window is centred and the number of moves taken. An episode begins with Ω as single face and ends when the mesh is solved or the move budget is exhausted. The mesh grows during an episode, so the observation is restricted to fixed-size template of nT the centres face loop, then breadth-first traversal of the next/previous/twin half-edges: pointers. Three integer arrays give each slots neighbours in the template, with two sentinel values distinguishing neighbour that exists but fell outside the window from one that does not exist because the half-edge lies on Ω. Actions are restricted to the template; par, the scores and the termination test are computed on the whole mesh. Each slot carries ten features. Chords leaving 2-gon on either side are masked out. desired and actual degree of the source and of the head vertex of the half-edge, and the number of sides of its face. Geometric: the half-edges length divided by the templates median, and the interior angles at its source and head as multiples of π/2. Flags: whether the source vertex lies on Ω, and whether it is corner of Ω. Degrees are clipped (vertices at eight, faces at fifteen) so that transient high-valence vertex cannot dominate the input scale. local window cannot say how far the whole mesh is from par, so the observation also carries global vector of seven scalars: the distance of the current irregularity from par, the total face defect, the number of odd-sided faces, par itself, the worst element quality, the mesh size relative to the window, and the face count, the first five divided by the number of faces so that each stays in its training range however large the mesh grows. The fraction of the move budget consumed is separate scalar. After each move the centre stays on its face until that face is quadrilateral, then moves to the most irregular face in view, or, when nothing irregular is in view, to the most irregular face or vertex in the whole mesh (Appendix B).

sections.title: 3.2 ACTIONS
sections.content: For half-edge with source u, three actions insert chord from to the vertex + 2 positions ahead of it in hs face loop, {0, 1, 2}, cutting sub-face of + 3 sides off the face that bounds; fourth splits hs edge with new vertex (Figure 2b). new vertex takes the generic desired degree g(v) of Section 2, so par is unchanged by every move. Invalid actions are masked: no chord may leave 2-gon, and no move may close face of at most four sides at boundary vertex that wants three or more edges (a corner of more than 135, including every flat boundary point) when both of its sides in that face lie on Ω: that element would have an angle of 180 or more there, and is degenerate whatever the smoother does. While our environment also supports deletions, we disable them to avoid free move-and-undo cycles. Between moves few Laplace smoothing sweeps keep the observed angles meaningful; the edit operations themselves fix only connectivity.

sections.title: 4.1 CONVOLUTION OVER N E X T, P R E V I O U S AND T W I N
sections.content: The observation is set of half-edges together with the three pointers that relate them, and the networks message passing follows those pointers. block reads, for every half-edge in the template, its own feature vector and those of its next, previous and twin, concatenates the four, and applies shared linear map, layer normalisation and LeakyReLU. neighbour that falls outside the window and one that does not exist because the half-edge lies on Ω are each replaced by their own learned vector, so the network can tell the edge of its view from the edge of the domain. Features are projected to common width and passed through residual stages of two blocks each; every block is one hop. No parameter is indexed by position in the template or by mesh size, so checkpoint applies unchanged to larger window or larger mesh, and configuration presents the same input wherever in the mesh it occurs. An ablation in Appendix compares this network with Transformer given the same features but not the adjacency.

sections.title: 4.2 FROM HALF-EDGES TO A MASKED ACTION DISTRIBUTION
sections.content: The global vector of Section 3.1 never enters message passing. The per-half-edge latents are pooled by mean and by maximum, concatenated with the global vector and the progress scalar, and mapped by two-layer MLP to context vector (Figure 4 in Appendix E). On the actor side each slots latent passes through shared layer, the context is added to every slot through shared linear map, and shared linear head emits four action logits per slot; flattened over the template and masked (Section 3.2), these form one categorical distribution over the action space. Because the context enters after the per-slot nonlinearity and the head is linear, it shifts every slots logits by the same vector: it can re-weight the four action types but cannot favour one half-edge over another. Where to act rests on the convolutions local features and the centring rule; what to do there is what the context can shift. The critic reads only the context, through its own two-layer MLP, since the value of state is property of the whole mesh and not of the half-edge the window happens to be centred on; the normalised return of Section 3.3 is what lets one such critic fit every domain size. The network has 96 channels, four residual stages and about 3.7 105 parameters.

sections.title: 5 TRAINING UNDER SPARSE REWARD
sections.content: Reaching par is sparse event. Under the MDP of Section 3, uniform random play reaches par on 3% of polygons with five or six sides, 2% of those with up to eight, and on none with more than eight. An explorer that has never reached par has never seen the only signal that distinguishes optimal from merely finished, and PPO from random initialisation reaches it on 7 of 96 domains after million steps (ablation in Appendix J). We overcome this exploration wall via behaviour cloning on families of meshes which are optimal by construction.

sections.title: 5.1 CERTIFIED INSTANCES WITHOUT SEARCH
sections.content: A polyomino, connected set of unit lattice cells, is already an at-par all-quadrilateral mesh of its outline. Rather than search for solution we start from one and undo it: backward walk removes edges and dissolves vertices, choosing only removals that invert legal forward move, until single face remains, and the reversed record is move-by-move solution in the agents own action space. Four seed families supply variety (polyominoes, annuli, polar meshes about hub, and pinwheel annuli, whose hole is rotated half step against its rim, shear in polar coordinates), and polyomino seeds are deformed by an affine map and per-corner jitter within its corners angle bins, which leaves its solution valid; moving corners across bin boundary yields instances whose bound is above zero (Appendix C).

sections.title: 5.2 CLONING, THEN REINFORCEMENT
sections.content: Replaying certified solution yields (observation, optimal move) pairs. Because independent moves commute, state usually has set of equally optimal moves; we record the set and minimise crossentropy against uniform distribution over it, together with value targets for the critic. The agent is cloned from 9,000 certified instances (about 187,000 pairs) for six epochs, reaching 93.7% top-one agreement with the certified sets, with model selection on development set of fifteen hand-made levels of simple primitives (Appendix I). PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) then continues from the cloned weights on mixture of generated domains (Appendix K) and certified ones: 35% of episodes start from freshly generated certified instance, so the policy keeps being asked to solve the problems cloning taught it and keeps meeting instances whose bound is not zero. Since the cloned value head was fit to returns on different scale from PPOs, and an advantage measured against it would be dominated by that offset, we first train the value head on frozen policy for forty epochs, and only after that run full PPO. Training runs with γ = λ = 1 and target KL of 0.03 for four million steps (Appendix F). The network is small enough that the whole recipe, generating the certified instances, cloning and four million PPO steps, takes about four hours on laptop (Apple M2, eight cores).

sections.title: 6.1 SETUP
sections.content: Domains. Training and evaluation outlines come from GEO2D, seeded generator of lattice-based mechanical parts: rectangular bases with cuts, additions and combs, optional 45 chamfers and interior holes. defined preset and seed determine domain exactly (Appendix K). All evaluation domains are straight-sided and unseen in training. The in-distribution set is 96 domains ranging in size from 8 to 24 boundary corners drawn from four families: rectilinear or chamfered, with or without holes. The larger-boundary set is 64 domains from the same four families with 25 to 50 corners, beyond anything seen in training. Every generated outline has par zero, but the faces the agent works through on the way do not: each intermediate polygon is sub-problem with its own bound, non-zero for 39% of them in distribution and 73% on the larger set (Appendix D). What is measured. Every method is judged on the mesh as delivered, after one pass of the same untangling smoother. We report, in this order: whether the mesh is all-quadrilateral; whether it is usable (shape quality 0.3); the excess over par, I(M) par(Ω) (tables give the median over 6 all-quadrilateral meshes); and whether it is at par, I(M) = par(Ω) with 0.1, the certificate of Section 2. Evaluation-time procedure. The same procedure is applied to every domain. Each is attempted five times one greedy rollout and four sampled with the move budget of Section 3.3 doubled to 6H0; every all-quadrilateral state along every attempt is untangled and scored, and the best is kept, ranked by all-quadrilateral first, then minimum quality, then closeness to par. If that mesh is below the quality bar, split-and-continue repair locates its worst corner, makes one of the environments own moves there vertex on the longer side of thin corner, chord across badly angled one and hands the state back to the policy to finish, for up to three rounds. Every count reported is the mean of this procedure over six rollout seeds on the in-distribution set and four on the larger set. Across seeds, all-quadrilateral does not move and usable moves by about one domain; at par moves by 1.3 of 96 and 4.1 of 64 (Appendix H). Baselines. Seven quadrilateral meshing configurations of Gmsh (Geuzaine & Remacle, 2009; Reberol et al., 2021) are run on the same domains and scored by the same criteria after the same smoother. Each is run at the element count the agent used on that domain, so that no method gains by refining its way to better score; those that cannot produce mesh that coarse are reported at their natural sizes. The elements column is the mean over methods all-quadrilateral meshes, and ours is that mean as multiple of ours. We also report head-to-head win rate: on each domain the agent wins if it produces an all-quadrilateral mesh and the baseline does not, loses in the reverse case, and otherwise wins on quality if its minimum quality is higher and on regularity if its excess over par is lower (equal values tie). This avoids comparing medians over the different subsets of domains each method completes.

sections.title: 6.2 MAIN RESULT
sections.content: The top block of Table 1 gives the in-distribution result. The agent produces an all-quadrilateral mesh on every one of the 96 domains, usable one on 95.7, and reaches the certified optimum on 90.2; the median excess over par is zero on every family. The Gmsh configurations that can be asked for the agents element count complete about half the domains, and those that complete all of them need three to fourteen times the elements to do so, and still carry median excess of 7.5 and 26. Across all seven configurations  (Table 6)  the certified optimum is reached three times in 672 attempts: quality-driven mesher has no notion of the bound. Head to head the agent wins on 90% of decided domains against BLOSSOM and 90% against FRONTAL-QUAD at matched count, 67% against QUASI-STRUCTURED at three times the elements, and 37% against BLOSSOM-FULL at fourteen times, the one case in which more elements buy Gmsh the better minimum quality more often than not. On regularity it wins on every decided domain against all four, at any of their element counts.

The agent completes every domain, clears the quality bar on 62.0, keeps median excess over par below one against Gmshs 39 at matched count, and reaches the certified optimum on 31.0, where no Gmsh configuration does. Head to head at matched count it wins on quality on 83% and 87% of decided domains against BLOSSOM and FRONTALQUAD, and on regularity on all of them, as against every configuration at any element count. sections.title: 6.4 CURVED BOUNDARIES
sections.content: We run the released agent, unchanged and never trained on curved boundary, on 96 domains of 824 corners with fillets and semicircular notches, with and without holes. Elements along arcs often fall below the quality bar, so we add test-time repair search. Full details are in Appendix L. Element quality along an arc can be judged against the arcs tangent or the chord connecting two vertices. For block decomposition, the tangent matters, since refinement will place vertices on the curved surface. However, we compute and report both metrics for the sake of comparison since it significantly affects the quality reading of Gmsh. The agent delivers median excess over par of 2 and reaches par on 37 of 96 domains, while every Gmsh configuration carries an excess of 10 to 32 and reaches par on at most 2; the agent wins on regularity on every decided domain against all four  (Table 2)  . It is usable on 95 of 96 against the tangents and 88 on chords. On chords Gmsh clears the bar far more often, on up to 79 with BLOSSOM-FULL at 4.4 the elements, but at matched element count the agent remains ahead of BLOSSOM and FRONTAL-QUAD. On 64 larger curved domains of 2550 corners (Appendix L) the 8 regularity result holds, median excess of 8 against 28 to 101, while the agent clears the quality bar on fewer domains than Gmsh configurations that use several times its elements.

sections.title: 7.1 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: The smoother is in the loop. The solved test untangles the mesh before judging it, and policy trained against that test relies on it; we score every method after the same smoother, but an agent that drew well-shaped mesh without one would be preferable. Runtime. Gmsh meshes domain in milliseconds; our unoptimised agent takes under second per in-distribution domain on laptop, seconds per larger domain, and minutes on the largest holed ones. Curved boundaries need search. The agent meshes curved domains close to the bound without retraining, but clearing the quality bar along arcs takes test-time repair search of up to ten minutes per domain (Section 6.4); policy that draws well-shaped elements along arcs without it remains open.

sections.title: 7.2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Learning to mesh. Learned quadrilateral meshing has so far learned where to place the next element: Pan et al. (2023) train soft actorcritic to make sequential meshing decisions, Tong et al. (2023) steer an advancing front with supervised and reinforcement learning, and, concurrently, Kalyan et al. (2026) pair geometric decomposition with all-quadrilateral generation in multi-agent framework. Our actions are instead edits on general polygonal half-edge mesh, and an episode ends at certificate of optimality rather than when front is consumed. Closest in objective is Narayanan et al. (2024), whose moves take one all-quadrilateral mesh to another toward ideal vertex degrees (contrasted in Section 1). Other learned mesh work optimises geometry or error rather than connectivity (Lorsung & Barati Farimani, 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Foucart et al., 2023; Thacher et al., 2025). Networks on mesh connectivity; learning backward from solutions. Edge and half-edge convolutions (Hanocka et al., 2019; Ludwig et al., 2023) analyse fixed triangle meshes; ours drives policy on polygonal mesh that changes every move, with action heads on the pointers it convolves over. Learning backward from solved state is established when there is one goal (McAleer et al., 2018; Agostinelli et al., 2019; Florensa et al., 2017; Resnick et al., 2018); here each domain has its own optimum, so certified optima are constructed and walked back to their boundary. Classical construction and the bound. Paving (Blacker & Stephenson, 1991), Q-Morph (Owen et al., 1999), medial-axis decomposition (Tam & Armstrong, 1991; Fogg et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2021) and the production meshers descended from them (Geuzaine & Remacle, 2009; Reberol et al., 2021) decide locally against quality heuristics; field-aligned methods (Bommes et al., 2009; Kalberer et al., 2007; Jakob et al., 2015; Ebke et al., 2013) optimise alignment to cross field. Neither targets topological bound. The bound itself is due to Peng & Wonka (2013) and Peng et al. (2014); we build on their work by making the bound the termination criterion of an MDP, reached by learned policy.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Quadrilateral block decomposition is an unusual reinforcement learning problem: the space of connectivities grows combinatorially with the boundary and the reward is sparse, yet every success carries certificate of optimality. Exploration almost never reaches that certificate, which stalls PPO from random start; cloning on optima that are trivial to construct gets past it, and PPO on generated domains improves on what cloning taught. The resulting decompositions are complete, usable and provably as regular as the domain permits, where production meshers at the same coarseness essentially never reach the bound, and remain nearly regular at twice the training scale and on curved boundaries the agent never saw in training.

sections.title: B THE CENTRING RULE
sections.content: Write the irregularity of face as sides 4 and the defect of vertex as deg(v) d(v), to the nearer option at tie corner. In the initial state the centre is the half-edge whose source vertex has the largest defect on the most irregular face. After each move: if the centres own face is not yet quadrilateral, the centre stays where it is and only the template around it is rebuilt. Otherwise, if any face meeting the current window is still irregular, the centre moves to one of maximal irregularity among those and, within it, to the half-edge whose source vertex has the largest defect. Only when nothing irregular remains in view does the rule consult the whole mesh, moving to face of maximal irregularity and its worst vertex; if every face is quadrilateral, the centre moves to the worst vertex anywhere.

sections.title: C CERTIFIED INSTANCES
sections.content: A polyomino is an at-par mesh of its outline because every interior vertex has degree four and every boundary vertex the degree its 90, 180 or 270 corner asks for. The four seed families contribute different structure. Polyominoes give rectilinear domains at par zero. Annuli give domains with hole; because the backward walk leaves the connecting slit in place, they arrive in the same singleface representation the agent meets at test time. Polar meshes of quadrilaterals about single hub give par 4 m. Polyomino seeds are then deformed by an affine map plus per-corner jitter, taken as far as the angle bins allow; seeds with hole and polar meshes are only mirrored (and rotated and scaled, which the normalised features do not see), so their variety comes from the construction itself. Holes in annuli are rotated relative to the outer boundary to create pinwheels. corners desired degree depends only on which bin its interior angle falls in, so the known solution stays valid on the skewed, irregular polygon. Redrawing an outline from prescribed corner angles is how instances with par above zero are produced: par is the total rounding error of the corner angles (Section 2), so moving corners 13 consistently across bin boundary yields an instance of par k. About third of the instances are of this kind. Every candidate is replayed through the environment and checked against the solved test of Section 3.3 before it enters the dataset. The last three rows are drawn with rotation and scale undone. Holed outlines keep one edge joining the hole to the outer boundary, so that the start state is single face. Shaded: faces that are not quadrilaterals. The trunk is per half-edge: convolved features pass through shared per-slot linear layer to the action head. sections.title: I THE DEVELOPMENT SET
sections.content: Model selection during cloning used fifteen hand-made levels L, T, and brackets, staircase, plus, triangle and pentagon, star, plates with square and triangular holes, gear, and three with curved sides each with known expert solution. They are small (three to ten corners), five of them are shapes the certified generator can itself produce, and they were never used for any number in Section 6. The released agent solves all fifteen greedily and twelve of the fourteen with known optimum in the experts move count; we report this as development score only.

sections.title: J ABLATIONS
sections.content: Cloning is necessary for PPO to learn. At one million PPO steps and the same seed, the recipe of Section 5 is at 91.8 usable and 76.2 at par of 96, where the same PPO run from freshly initialised network completes 73.5 but passes the quality bar on 10 and reaches the bound on 7, with median excess over par of four; on the larger domains nothing it completes is usable (Table 9, right). Cloning alone completes 92.8 and is usable on 73.5 but reaches par on only 22.3; million PPO steps from it take that to 76.2. This is the exploration wall of Section 5: without supply of solved instances the policy rarely sees the event that the reward targets. DCEL connectivity has to be an input. We train Transformer encoder with the same parameter count, features, action space, data, reward and budget, whose input is breadth-first serialisation of the template with positional encoding of slot order. This is lossy serialisation of the adjacency. It reaches par on about half as many domains as the convolution, and already lagged at the end of cloning (Table 9, left). We read this as difference in what the input identifies rather than in capacity, and expect an attention model masked or biased by next, previous and twin to do comparably well. Run-to-run variance. Two training seeds of the released configuration without its quality term, and two seeds of the whole pipeline (new certified instances, cloning and PPO), differ in distribution by at most 0.7 domains on usable and 2.7 on at par; on the larger set, by 35 on usable and about 10 on at par. Out of distribution the seed spread is about five domains, above the evaluation-seed spread of Table 8, so the larger-boundary numbers should be read as ranges. 18 Table 9: Left: domains at par of the 96 in-distribution domains, best of five, at matched 2M steps under an earlier configuration of the recipe, mean of two seeds. Right: PPO from fresh network, cloning only, and cloning then PPO, at 1M PPO steps, seed 1, best of five at the default move budget and without repair. extractor params at par DCEL, 4 layers Transf., 4 layers 299k 300k 94.5 51.5 set 96 64 training all-quad usable excess at par PPO clone clone + PPO PPO clone clone + PPO 73.5 92.8 95.5 13.5 32.5 51.5 10.2 73.5 91.8 0.0 0.0 14.0 4 2 0 16.75 6.6 2 7.2 22.3 76.2 0.0 0.0 16. GENERATING DOMAINS, AND DRAWING THE MESH Outlines. Training and evaluation domains come from GEO2D, seeded generator of lattice-based mechanical parts. shape begins as an occupancy raster on an integer lattice base rectangle, then rectangular cuts, additions and combs anchored on the current boundary, each kept only if the material stays connected and free of pinches and voids and tracing that raster gives counterclockwise lattice polygon, to which corner modifiers (45 chamfers for the straight-sided families; fillets and semicircular notches for the curved ones of Appendix L) and interior holes with at least one lattice unit of clearance are applied with exact geometry. One lattice unit is by construction the smallest feature, so domain of ratio fits in an box and admits uniform mesh of unit size, which keeps element counts comparable across sampled set. preset fixes the parameters and seed determines domain exactly, so training distribution and held-out evaluation set are specified by preset and two seed ranges. The larger-boundary set also caps the ratio of longest to shortest boundary edge at ten, so drop there measures size rather than geometric extremity. Smoothing. The edit operations of Section 3.2 set connectivity and say nothing about where nodes sit, so every geometric property of the result is the smoothers doing. Between moves we run few Laplacian sweeps, which are cheap and keep the observed angles meaningful. Where quality decides something the solved test, and every reported number the mesh is instead untangled: for each free node condition-number objective over its adjacent corners is minimised by Newton steps, with 2 + δ2)/2 so that an inverted corner is pushed the corner Jacobian entering through h(J) = (J + back out rather than sending the objective to infinity (Escobar et al., 2003). The corners of Ω never move; nodes the agent inserted on boundary edge slide along it toward the same objective, and slide is accepted only if the worst adjacent corner does not get worse (Freitag, 1997). The same smoother, with the same settings, is applied to every method before it is scored.

sections.title: L CURVED BOUNDARIES
sections.content: The bound on curved domains. Section 2 states the bound for polygons, but its proof uses no straightness. vertex inside an arc has θv = π by tangent continuity, so the only geometry entering equation 2 is again the set of corner angles: smooth arc contributes to par exactly as straight edge does. square and disc are both topological discs, but the squares four corners give par = 0 while the disc, with none, has par = 4. The repair search. Section 6.4 runs the released agent, trained only on straight-sided domains, with no change to its weights, observation or action space. The domains are the four curved suites, with fillets and semicircular notches: 48 each at 824 and 2550 corners, with and without holes (16 for the holed larger suite), every arc discretised at 45. The agents five attempts of Section 6.1, at the doubled move budget, supply pool of all-quadrilateral states, each untangled with the arcs tangents. The search then repeats: take the most regular states still below the quality bar; at the worst element of each apply one edit, either refining the quadrilateral sheet through it (all-quadrilateral in and out, every new vertex at its want, so the excess over par is unchanged), or inserting vertex on one of its sides or chord across it and letting the agent finish the mesh; untangle the results and add 19 them to the pool. It stops after 600 s. The answer is the mesh with the lowest excess over par among those that clear the bar, ties going to fewer elements, so that refinement is kept only when it buys the bar. The row without the search in Table 2 selects from the same pool by quality first, as Section 6.1 does. The search judges quality with each corner on an arc measured against the arcs tangent; this is consistent with block decomposition wherein refinement will add new vertices on the arc and not on the chord. However, Gmsh often fails the quality bar when measured on tangents, therefore we report quality measured by the tangent as well as the chord for fairness.
